Name: reversal_asymmetry_mechanism
Title: One-Way Streets: The Mechanistic Basis of the Reversal Curse
Short Hypothesis: Forward relations ('A's capital is B') and their inverse ('B is the capital of A') are stored and accessed asymmetrically because the subject-position enrichment binds attributes in one direction only; the inverse query lacks a subject locus carrying the needed association. This predicts that reverse recall fails not from missing storage but from missing directional access, testable by probing.
Related Work: Berglund et al. (2023) document the reversal curse behaviorally and argue models trained on 'A is B' do not infer 'B is A'. Explanations remain largely behavioral. We provide a mechanistic account grounded in the asymmetric, subject-anchored enrichment established by causal tracing, predicting where the inverse association is (and is not) decodable and why.
Abstract: Language models that reliably answer 'The capital of France is ___' often fail at 'Paris is the capital of ___', a phenomenon called the reversal curse. We test a mechanistic explanation: factual associations are written into the residual stream at the subject token during pretraining, producing a directional key-value binding from subject to object; the inverse query presents the object as subject and finds no locus carrying the backward association. We predict that (i) the forward object is decodable from the forward-subject position but the forward subject is NOT decodable from the object position at matched layers, (ii) causal tracing for the reverse query shows no analogous enrichment peak, and (iii) fine-tuning that explicitly writes the reverse association restores a symmetric decodable locus. We test these on synthetic and natural facts across models, using attribute probes and causal tracing in both directions, and we measure the decodability asymmetry as a quantitative index of the curse. We further ask whether relations that are naturally bidirectional in text (spouse-of) show reduced asymmetry, supporting a data-directionality account. The results explain the reversal curse as a directional access failure rooted in how associations are physically written, and predict which relations and training interventions can mitigate it.
Experiments: 1. Construct matched forward/reverse factual pairs (synthetic 'A is B' facts plus natural relations). 2. Train direction-specific attribute probes; measure decodability of object-from-subject vs subject-from-object across layers. 3. Run causal tracing for both directions; compare enrichment peaks. 4. Compute an asymmetry index and correlate with behavioral reversal accuracy. 5. Fine-tune on reverse statements and re-measure decodability and behavior. 6. Compare symmetric relations (spouse) vs asymmetric (capital). Metrics: directional probe accuracy, tracing peak magnitude, asymmetry index, post-finetune symmetry.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Natural relations vary in text directionality, confounding comparisons; synthetic facts control this but may not transfer. Probes may fail to find associations that are present but non-linearly encoded. Fine-tuning could introduce new mechanisms rather than reveal the original. Multi-token entities complicate probing.
